sources.title: Ryazan Historical and Architectural Museum: archaeology of Old Ryazan
sources.note: Old capital, destruction in December 1237 and attempts to rebuild. Hoards discovered near the cathedral in 1822 and in a house oven in 1950. Outdated total of sixteen hoards omitted.

sources.title: Zavyalov and Terekhova: Blacksmithing in the Grand Principality of Ryazan
sources.note: Pereyaslavl Ryazansky section opens with final incorporation of Ryazan principality into Moscow in 1521. Exact indexed institutional passage verified; direct PDF too large for web tool.

sources.title: Institute of Archaeology: Old Ryazan expedition, 2020
sources.note: Excavation 47: domestic and craft plots, clay ovens, ice cellar caption, jewellery tools, coin pendants and green-glazed toys. The centaur die’s provenance is not asserted.

sources.title: Institute of Archaeology online museum: chess piece from Old Ryazan
sources.note: Bone piece from excavation 47 in 2020, dated to the late twelfth or first half of the thirteenth century; abstract elephant with possible tusks.

sources.title: Institute of Archaeology: archaeological treasures of 2021
sources.note: Isady hoard, four kilometres east of Old Ryazan and outside the city. Distinct from the unrelated first-millennium Suzdal hoard discussed in the article’s first half.

sources.title: Ryazan Museum newspaper, September 2021, number 4 (50)
sources.note: Printed pages 2-5: birchbark drawing, Vvedensky toys and street, food plants and animal remains. Later sixteenth/seventeenth-century craft sites and the 1620 street are excluded. Gramoty supersedes the preliminary letter reading.

sources.title: Gramoty: Pereyaslavl Ryazansky birchbark document 1
sources.note: Scholarly transcription, conventional date 1450-1500, prophecy associated with Paschalia. No published English translation on the page; one complete word is literally translated here.

sources.title: UNESCO: Churches of the Pskov School of Architecture
sources.note: Architectural forms, local materials, gardens and the fifteenth/sixteenth-century peak; property also includes buildings outside the republic period.

sources.title: Lawrence N. Langer: Pskov Judicial Charter, Encyclopedia of Russian History
sources.note: Signed academic reference entry; inheritance, maintenance of parents, wage claims, and independence from 1348. Rules are distinguished from universal practice.

sources.title: Presidential Library: Pskov Judicial Charter manuscript
sources.note: Library of the Academy of Sciences manuscript 34.2.31; surviving copies postdate the republic. Competing compilation dates and modern division into 120 articles.

sources.title: Bank of Russia Museum: Pskov
sources.note: Minting from 1425, denga and chetverettsa, Dovmont and leopard designs; distinguish later Muscovite mint output.

sources.title: Gramoty: Pskov birchbark document 6
sources.note: Conventional date 1260-1280, with possible earlier shift. Historical transcription and R. Kovalev/Jos Schaeken translations. Quoted greeting uses the segmented scholarly transcription.

sources.title: Gramoty: Pskov birchbark document 7
sources.note: Conventional date 1280-1300; broader external dating, preference for early fourteenth century. Cloth shipment and transport fee, Russian translation.

sources.title: Russian Historical Society: removal of Pskov’s assembly bell in 1510
sources.note: Neutral chronology only: Vasily III abolished the assembly and posadnik offices, removed the bell and imposed governors. National-unification rhetoric not adopted.

sources.title: Moscow Kremlin Museums: history of the Dormition Cathedral
sources.note: Indexed institutional text: Ivan IV crowned 16 January 1547; coronation and regalia.

sources.title: State Historical Museum: Saint Basil’s Cathedral
sources.note: Construction 1555-1561 to commemorate victory over Kazan; later additions and interiors must not be dated wholly to Ivan IV.

sources.title: Presidential Library: the first Romanov tsar, source collection
sources.note: Famine, civil disorder, intervention and election of Mikhail in 1613. Neutral facts only, no adoption of monarchist historical rhetoric.

sources.title: Great Russian Encyclopedia: Assembly Code of 1649
sources.note: 2015 academic encyclopedia, hereditary serfdom and unlimited pursuit of fugitives.

sources.title: Denis J. B. Shaw: Reconnoitring Russia
sources.note: Printed p. 51 and preceding discussion, seventeenth-century Siberian expansion, yasak, violence and Pacific journeys. Avoid older Library of Congress essay with erroneous Kazan/Astrakhan dates.

sources.title: Russian State Library: Moscow Apostle, 1564
sources.note: First precisely dated Moscow printed book, production time and two-colour process. Print-run estimate omitted.

sources.title: Institute of Archaeology: excavations in Moscow’s Kislovskaya quarter
sources.note: 2025 excavation report; sixteenth/seventeenth-century preserved-food suppliers, cellar pits, seventeenth-century glazed stove tiles. Do not use later bird spool or portrait tile as tsardom objects.

sources.title: Kolomenskoye Museum: Water Tower
sources.note: 1670s structure; source below tower, mechanical lifting, barrel and wooden pipes. Mechanism alternatives kept open.

sources.title: Military Medical Museum: functions of the Apothecary Chancery
sources.note: Museum’s historical explanation, 1654 school with thirty pupils and translation-assisted training. Displayed diagram is a 1949 teaching aid, not a seventeenth-century artefact.

sources.title: Russian State Library: Karion Istomin’s primer, Moscow 1696
sources.note: RSL MK H-71, proof copy. Preface wording quoted by library, normalized Cyrillic transcription, translated literally here. Alphabet, syllables, twenty-copy edition and acrostic on leaf 78.

sources.title: Presidential Library: Peter I accepts the imperial title, 1721
sources.note: 22 October/2 November 1721; Treaty of Nystad and change of title.

sources.title: Arkadii Zhukovsky: Kyiv principality, Encyclopedia of Ukraine
sources.note: Regional principality distinguished from all Kyivan Rus; continued after 1240; Lithuanian rule 1362, abolition 1394, restoration 1440, final transformation 1471.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Kyiv voivodeship
sources.note: 1471 voivodeship replaced the principality.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Podil
sources.note: Medieval harbour, market and artisan districts, with later centuries excluded.

sources.title: Museum of the History of the Tithe Church: glass-jewellery workshops of Podil
sources.note: 2022 museum archaeological synthesis: twelfth/early thirteenth-century workshop context, ingots, crucibles, manufacture and workshop colour groups.

sources.title: M. Sergeeva: Bone and antler tools in Kyiv Rus, Middle Dnipro case study
sources.note: 2025 scholarly article, abstract and dating. Regional evidence explicitly labelled Middle Dnipro; variable functions of pointed bone tools and skates preserved.

sources.title: UNESCO: Saint Sophia and Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra
sources.note: Eleventh-century cathedral decoration and monastery foundation; later Baroque buildings explicitly not treated as medieval.

sources.title: Viacheslav Korniienko interview: the graffiti of Saint Sophia
sources.note: Primary interview with reserve’s research director, 3 February 2021. Priest tallies, interpreted school exercises, and exact quoted Church Slavonic prayer formula. Institutional genealogy and sweeping modern national-language claims not adopted.

sources.title: Arkadii Zhukovsky: Principality of Galicia-Volhynia
sources.note: Academic encyclopedia, foundation in 1199, dynastic politics and transition after 1340.

sources.title: Pavlo Hrytsak: Danylo Romanovych
sources.note: Crown in 1253, submission to Batu in 1246, failed western alliance and enforced demolition of fortifications.

sources.title: Gazda, Bevz and Gołub: Natural stone in King Daniel’s castle at Chełm
sources.note: TEKA 18(2), 2022, pp. 41-54. Excavators’ material analysis; pp. 42-45 on green stone and its properties.

sources.title: Gazda and Bevz: Natural and artificial stone at Daniel’s residence
sources.note: Architectural Studies 5(2), 2019, pp. 92-104. Abstract reports experimental material identification; interpretation explicitly attributed.

sources.title: Arkadii Zhukovsky: Galician-Volhynian Chronicle
sources.note: Composition, Galician and Volhynian sections, later chronological redaction and princely viewpoint.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Ukraine: Volodymyr Vasylkovych
sources.note: Library and patronage. Does not claim general literacy or use the entry’s disputed precise death date.

sources.title: Lviv Polytechnic: researchers and the Ancient Zvenyhorod project
sources.note: Institutional report quoting archaeologists Vasyl Petryk and Nataliia Voitseshchuk. Indexed text verifies preserved wood, footwear, tableware, glass jewellery and workshop quarter. Direct page returned an error.

sources.title: Gramoty: Zvenyhorod Galician birchbark document 2
sources.note: Conventional dating 1120-1140, explicitly earlier than the united principality. Scholarly transcription and Kovalev/Schaeken translations.

sources.title: Mykhailo Zhdan: Polatsk principality
sources.note: Academic historical entry; river trade, dynastic division, Lithuanian incorporation in 1307 and surviving autonomy.

sources.title: G. V. Shtykhov: Cities of the Polotsk Land, ninth to thirteenth centuries
sources.note: Minsk, 1978, Institute of History of the Belarusian Academy of Sciences; digitized scholarly monograph. Printed pp. 119-120, 135. Regional and later thirteenth-century examples are labelled.

sources.title: L. V. Alekseev: Lazar Bogsha, twelfth-century master jeweller
sources.note: Scholarly article reprint with 1896 photographs and drawings. Section 2 describes materials, custom enamels and inscription, including exact transcribed word злото. Ethnic-origin speculation is not adopted.

sources.title: P. A. Rappoport: Church of the Saviour, Euphrosyne’s monastery
sources.note: Reprint from Russian Architecture of the Tenth to Thirteenth Centuries; structural survey distinguishes surviving medieval fabric and later alterations.

sources.title: MNRHU: restoration of the Saviour church at Polotsk
sources.note: Restorers’ institutional account: removing and preserving eighteenth/nineteenth-century overpainting while revealing twelfth-century frescoes. Indexed text checked; direct page failed.

sources.title: Polotsk tourism: religious monuments
sources.note: Local institutional tourism resource: Euphrosyne’s convent, twelfth-century church and 1161 commission. Avoids presenting the modern recreated cross as the lost original.

sources.title: Polotsk tourism: Saint Sophia Cathedral
sources.note: Mid-eleventh-century construction and surviving foundations, apses and frescoes; extensive subsequent rebuilding.

sources.title: Mikhail Borisenok: Vladimir-Suzdal principality
sources.note: Signed historical reference: rise, fragmentation, Horde authority, Moscow’s acquisition of Vladimir and inheritance in 1389. Full indexed text checked; direct fetch failed.

sources.title: Great Russian Encyclopedia: Rus principalities in the 1130s to 1230s
sources.note: Academic synthesis, section on Suzdal: Volga trade, fertile Opolye and political rise.

sources.title: Fedorina, Makarov, Milovanov and Baranov: medieval Suzdal
sources.note: Suzdal archaeological monograph, city chapter, printed p. 247: continued growth after 1157, nearby villages and gardens. Indexed page checked; large PDF direct fetch failed.

sources.title: N. A. Baranov: Combs from archaeological research in Suzdal
sources.note: KSIA 278 (2025), pp. 308-327, DOI 10.25681/IARAS.0130-2620.278.308-327. Full indexed article checked: materials, composite construction, chronology and workshops.

sources.title: Makarov, Gaidukov and Milovanov: Yuri and Gregory’s seals from Suzdal
sources.note: 2024 institutional excavation report. Yuri’s personal sign; earlier Gregory notary seal, Greek errors and possible origin. No certain employer asserted.

sources.title: UNESCO: White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal
sources.note: Twelfth/thirteenth-century architecture, white limestone, relief carvings, Assumption Cathedral and later Rublev frescoes.

sources.title: Gippius and Mikheev: Assassins of the Great Prince Andrey
sources.note: Author-hosted full article, Slověne 9(2), 2020, pp. 63-102, DOI 10.31168/2305-6754.2020.9.2.3. Printed p. 87 normalized transcription and Russian translation; dating discussion proposes 1175-1176.

batchIdentityNotes.note: Shared narrative is for the same historical principality and explicitly separates Old Ryazan from Pereyaslavl Ryazansky. The imported 1279 Ryazan polygon is grossly overbroad (21.357-46.043E,47.384-62.209N) and must not be accepted as authentic extent. The 1492 polygon is also broad; the 1500 polygon is compact near Ryazan. No polygon correction proposed without a source. Incorporation in 1521 precedes the map endpoint of 1530.

Imported geometry is around Pskov. Coverage 1492-1530 extends beyond historical annexation in 1510. Earlier letters are explicitly dated background to the republic; no claim that its institutions survived until 1530.

Decoded geometry expands east across Siberia and reaches 180 degrees longitude in the 1715 snapshot. Imported 1530-1783 is not the tsardom’s historical lifespan: 1547 coronation, 1721 imperial transition. Existing Grand Duchy of Moscow and Russia cards are distinct phases; no shared-card substitution.

1200-1279 imported geography is the regional Kyiv principality, not all Kyivan Rus. Card focuses on twelfth/thirteenth-century material with explicitly dated earlier architecture and later institutional ending. Bone-tool evidence is regional, not assigned wholesale to one Kyiv excavation.

Imported coverage 1200-1279 is shorter than historical state chronology. Decoded southern reach to 45.057 latitude is implausibly broad and must not be endorsed. Zvenyhorod letter and preserved household evidence are explicitly identified as earlier regional background.

Imported 1100-1200 geometry is centred on Polotsk and represents a limited map phase, not the whole political lifespan. Later thirteenth-century domestic finds and earlier cathedral are explicitly dated; no modern-state identity substituted.

Imported 1200-1279 geometry covers northeastern Rus. Historical narrative distinguishes pre-Mongol unity, later fragmentation and Moscow’s hereditary acquisition by 1389; no single disappearance in 1279. Pre-1157 seals and post-1279 Rublev paintings are explicitly dated context.
